V03-E-001: Planners sometimes lay out the paths of a new park before anyone has walked there, guessing where visitors will want to go. Within months, worn strips of bare earth often appear across the lawns, marking the shortcuts that people actually prefer. Some designers now treat these desire paths as information, waiting a season before paving and then surfacing the routes that feet have already chosen. The approach accepts that the users of a space can reveal its needs more reliably than a drawing made in advance. Many city parks were laid out on land that had once been private estates, hunting grounds or marshes.
V03-E-002: Countries that import much of their television tend to settle on one of two habits: dubbing foreign programmes into the local language or subtitling them. Dubbing lets viewers watch without reading, but it replaces the actors' voices and often bends the dialogue to match the movement of their lips. Subtitling keeps the original performance intact, at the cost of asking the audience to divide its attention between the picture and the text. Neither choice is simply better, since each gives up one valuable thing in order to keep another. Television arrived in different countries at very different times, and in some it remained a state monopoly for decades.
V03-E-003: Body mass index, calculated from a person's weight and height, is popular because it is cheap, quick and needs no special equipment. Its simplicity, however, means that it cannot tell muscle from fat, so a heavily muscled athlete may be classed as overweight. Nor does it reveal where fat is stored, although fat around the abdomen is generally thought to carry greater risk than fat elsewhere. The index is therefore best treated as a rough screening tool for populations rather than as a verdict on any one person's health. Regular physical activity, even brisk walking for half an hour a day, is widely recommended for adults of every weight.
V03-E-004: When enough people in a community are immune to an infection, the disease struggles to find new hosts and outbreaks tend to fade out. This protection extends to those who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborn babies or patients whose immune systems are weakened. The share of the population that must be immune depends on how contagious the disease is; the more easily it spreads, the higher the threshold. For this reason, a small fall in vaccination rates can matter far more for a highly contagious disease than for a mildly contagious one. The first vaccines were developed long before scientists understood what viruses actually were.
V03-E-005: People tend to grow fonder of things simply because they have encountered them before, even when they cannot recall the earlier encounters. A melody heard several times in the background, for instance, is often rated as more pleasant than one heard only once. Advertisers make use of this tendency when they repeat a brand name or a jingle far more often than any new information would justify. In such cases familiarity is quietly mistaken for genuine merit. Memory for faces is generally better than memory for names, which is why people often recognise someone they cannot name.
V03-E-006: Beginners in mathematics often learn more from studying fully worked examples than from attempting problems on their own straight away. When a novice tries to solve a problem unaided, much of their attention goes into searching for a method, leaving little for understanding why it works. A worked example removes that search and lets the learner concentrate on the structure of the solution. As skill grows, however, the benefit shrinks, and practice without a model eventually becomes the better use of time. Anxiety about mathematics, a feeling of tension when faced with numbers, troubles many students and some adults throughout their lives.
V03-E-007: In a busy emergency department, patients are not seen in the order in which they arrive but in the order of how urgently they need care. A nurse usually makes a quick assessment of each newcomer, checking breathing, pulse, pain and other warning signs. On that basis the patient is placed in a priority category, so that someone with chest pain may be seen before a person who has waited longer with a sprained wrist. The system can feel unfair to those kept waiting, but it is designed so that delay falls on those who can best afford it. Ambulance crews are trained to keep patients stable during the journey and to pass on key details when they arrive at the hospital.
V03-E-008: Many early writing systems ran words together without spaces or punctuation, leaving readers to work out the divisions for themselves. Such texts were usually read aloud, and the reader supplied the pauses and emphasis from knowledge of the language. As silent, private reading spread, marks that showed the structure of a sentence on the page became more and more useful. Punctuation thus began as a guide to the voice and gradually became a guide to the eye. Spelling in many languages has changed more slowly than pronunciation, so that written words often preserve sounds that are no longer spoken.
V03-E-009: It is often assumed that sign languages are simply spoken languages translated into gestures, word for word. In fact, established sign languages have their own grammar, using space, movement and facial expression to mark relations that speech marks with word order or endings. This independence is why two countries that share a spoken language can use sign languages that the signers of each find largely unintelligible. Recognising sign languages as full languages rather than as codes has consequences for the way deaf children are taught. Facial expression also carries emotion in spoken conversation, and listeners rely on it more than they usually realise.
V03-E-010: Many readers treat a dictionary as a rulebook that tells them how words ought to be used. Most modern lexicographers, however, regard their job as describing the language people really speak and write, which they do by gathering and studying vast numbers of real examples. When a new sense of a word becomes common enough, it enters the dictionary, whatever purists may think of it. The authority that readers grant the dictionary is therefore, in a sense, borrowed from the speakers whose habits it records. Older dictionaries were often compiled by a single scholar over many years, whereas modern ones are usually produced by large teams.
V03-E-011: Children who begin school in a language they do not speak at home face two tasks at once: learning the language and learning through it. When early lessons are given in the mother tongue, the second task can begin at once, because the child already understands what the teacher says. Reading skills built in a familiar language also tend to carry over, so that learning to read a second language later becomes easier. The case for mother-tongue instruction is thus not a rejection of other languages but a claim about the order in which they are best learned. Children who grow up hearing two languages at home sometimes mix words from both in a single sentence, a habit that usually fades with age.
V03-E-012: Sorting pupils into classes by ability is often defended on the ground that teachers can pitch lessons more precisely to a narrower range of learners. The evidence is more mixed than this argument suggests, because gains for the top groups are frequently offset by losses for those placed lower down. Pupils in lower groups may be given less demanding work and come to see themselves as weak, which can lower their effort further. Whether grouping helps, then, depends less on the sorting itself than on whether lower groups are taught with the same ambition as the rest. Some schools group pupils by age, while others run mixed-age classes in which older children help the younger ones.
V03-E-013: Many people think an open-book paper must be a soft option, since a candidate with the textbook at hand can presumably just copy out what is needed. In practice, a well-designed open-book paper asks questions whose answers cannot be found on any page, such as applying a principle to an unfamiliar case. Students who have not understood the material soon discover that the book is of little help under time pressure. What the format removes is the reward for memorising, not the need for preparation. Examinations taken at home without supervision raise obvious questions about whether the work submitted is really the student's own.
V03-E-014: Fever is usually treated as something to be brought down, yet a raised temperature is part of the body's response to infection rather than merely a symptom of it. Many microbes multiply less efficiently at higher temperatures, and some immune cells appear to work more effectively when the body is warmer. This has led some physicians to question the habit of reducing every moderate fever with medication. They do not deny that very high fevers can be dangerous; their point is that comfort and recovery are not always served by the same treatment. A thermometer placed under the tongue usually gives a slightly different reading from one placed in the ear or under the arm.
V03-E-015: Many of the world's great river deltas are sinking, and in some places the land is falling faster than the sea is rising. Part of the cause is the pumping of groundwater, which allows the soft sediments beneath delta cities to compact. Another is the dams built upstream, which trap the sediment that rivers once carried down to rebuild the delta in each flood season. Because these causes are largely of human making, they are, unlike the rising sea, within reach of local policy. Sea levels rise unevenly across the globe, because ocean currents, winds and the pull of the great ice sheets differ from one region to another.
V03-E-016: Charging drivers to enter a crowded city centre at busy hours is often opposed as a tax on people who have no choice but to drive. Its advocates reply that road space at peak times is a scarce good, and that giving it away free simply rations it by queuing instead of by price. A modest charge persuades some drivers to travel earlier, share a car or take a bus, and the traffic that remains moves faster. The fairness objection is not thereby answered, but it shifts to the question of how the money raised is spent. Many cities have also introduced low-emission zones, which charge or ban the most polluting vehicles regardless of the time of day.
V03-E-017: A person in distress in a crowded place is not necessarily more likely to receive help than one who collapses on a quiet street. Each onlooker may assume that someone else has already acted, or is better placed to act, and the responsibility spreads so thin that no one takes it up. Onlookers also watch one another for cues, and when everyone appears calm, each concludes that the situation must not be an emergency. Singling out one person and asking them directly for help can therefore break the deadlock, because it hands the responsibility back to an individual. People are generally more willing to help someone who resembles them, whether in age, dress or manner of speaking.
V03-E-018: Once we know how events turned out, we tend to believe that we could have predicted the outcome all along. Information that pointed towards the actual result seems, in retrospect, to have been obvious, while the signals that pointed elsewhere fade from memory. This distortion makes us harsh judges of decision-makers, who are blamed for failing to see what became clear only afterwards. A fair assessment of a decision must therefore ask what was knowable at the time, not what is known now. Experts in some fields make forecasts that are barely more accurate than chance, yet they remain confident in them.
V03-E-019: People routinely underestimate how long their own projects will take, even when they know that similar projects in the past ran late. The error arises partly because planners imagine the specific steps of the task and picture them going smoothly, leaving no room for the delays that usually intrude. Interestingly, people are often more realistic about other people's projects, which they see from the outside, without the vivid detail of each step. This suggests a remedy: before planning the details, ask how long comparable projects have actually taken, and adjust from there. Deadlines set by others often lead people to work harder in the final days before them than at any earlier point.
V03-E-020: Suppose a ship has its timbers renewed piece by piece over many years until none of the original wood remains; it seems natural to say that the same ship is still sailing. Yet if someone gathered the discarded planks and reassembled them, that reconstructed vessel would also have a strong claim to be the original. The puzzle suggests that our idea of sameness combines two criteria, continuity of form and history and continuity of material, which normally coincide and come apart only in unusual cases. Asking which ship is 'really' the original may then be less a question about the world than about which criterion we have reason to favour for a given purpose. This shows that the material of an object, rather than its history, is what finally fixes its identity.
V03-E-021: The question of whether animals matter morally is often framed as a question about intelligence, as though cleverer creatures deserved more consideration. But the capacity that seems most relevant to how a being may be treated is not the ability to reason but the ability to suffer. A creature that can feel pain has an interest in not being hurt, whether or not it can solve puzzles or use tools. On this view, the hard questions concern which animals can suffer and how much, and these are questions about evidence that tests of intelligence cannot settle. What deserves protection, some argue, is not the individual animal but the species, whose loss is final in a way that a single death is not.
V03-E-022: A familiar argument holds that duties to the unborn are impossible, because a duty must be owed to someone and the unborn are, as yet, no one at all. The argument proves too much, however: someone who buried a device set to explode in a hundred years would plainly be doing wrong, though every eventual victim is yet unborn. What makes the act wrong is not the present existence of its victims but the foreseeable harm it will cause to whoever comes to exist. If that is right, the absence of present persons is no bar to obligations concerning pollution, debt or the depletion of resources whose effects arrive long after us. Some economists hold that benefits in the future should count for less than benefits now, simply because they lie further ahead in time.
V03-E-023: Ordinary morality distinguishes between what we are required to do and what it would be admirable, but not obligatory, to do. A passer-by who pulls a drowning child from shallow water does only what is required, whereas one who dives into a freezing river at great risk does more than duty demands. Some moral theories have trouble with this distinction, because if one should always do the best act available, no act can go beyond what is required. Defenders of the ordinary view reply that a morality leaving no room for heroism beyond duty would ask too much of people and leave too little to their own choice. Heroic acts are often performed on impulse, and those who perform them commonly insist afterwards that anyone would have done the same.
V03-E-024: Memories of where we were when we heard shocking news feel unusually vivid, and people hold them with great confidence. Yet when researchers have questioned people soon after such an event and again years later, the two accounts have often differed in important details. What sets these memories apart, it seems, is the certainty and feeling with which they are recalled rather than any special fidelity to what happened. Their vividness may owe less to the moment itself than to the many times the story has been retold and rehearsed since. Because such memories are shared by so many people, they offer historians a valuable record of how ordinary people lived through great events.
V03-E-025: The regular street grid is often criticised as a monotonous imposition, the work of surveyors who drew straight lines without regard to the ground. Yet the grid's indifference to particular sites is also what made it useful to growing cities, since land could be divided, sold and built on before anyone knew what would stand there. The same blocks could hold houses, then shops, then offices, without the plan of the streets having to change. What critics read as a lack of design may thus be better understood as a design for uncertainty. Whether a street is pleasant to walk along depends more on the width of its pavements and the shade of its trees than on the geometry of the plan.
